cues.text: Section seven is a practical lab on relational schema design.
Let's begin with the scenario.
VitalNet operates clinical hubs in Kano and Enugu, and administrative nodes in Port Harcourt and Uyo.
The problem is that its legacy patient records are fragmented.
That fragmentation creates redundancy, meaning the same facts are stored in several places, and it creates poor interoperability, meaning the different systems struggle to work together.
Your task in this lab has several steps, and the order matters.
First, build a relational schema, similar to the example above.
Second, insert synthetic data: synthetic clinics, synthetic patients and synthetic visits.
Synthetic simply means made up for testing, not real patient information.
Third, verify your joins, so you confirm that related rows from the different tables really do connect correctly.
Fourth, test two kinds of bad input: invalid foreign keys, and duplicate identifiers.
The expected behaviour is this.
An invalid reference, such as a visit pointing at a patient that does not exist, should be rejected.
A duplicate primary key, such as two patients with the same identifier, should also be rejected.
Those rejections are the database enforcing referential integrity and key uniqueness for you.
There is one more design instruction.
Keep high-volume wearable observations separable from core patient identity.
Wearable devices produce a great deal of readings.
If they are tangled into the central patient table, that table becomes heavy and hard to manage, so they belong in a separate structure that links back to the patient.
Finally, a caution from the source.
The examples are teaching SQL, not claimed executed results.
So treat them as illustrations of what should happen, not as output that was actually run.
Now, the heading: additional design revision.
Let's revise some core ideas.
A schema describes the structure of the database, while an instance is its current contents.
Think of the schema as the blueprint, and the instance as the house as it stands today, furnished with whatever data is in it right now.
The schema changes rarely.
The instance changes constantly.
Next, data independence.
This means the schema and the storage can evolve without unnecessarily breaking the applications that use the database.
You can reorganise how data is stored, and the applications keep working.
Then there is the data dictionary.
Use it to record definitions, types, owners and constraints.
It is the documented reference describing what each piece of data means, what type it is, who is responsible for it, and what rules apply to it.
Now deployment.
In a three-tier deployment, distinguish the database server from the application tier and the presentation tier.
The database server holds and manages the data.
The application tier holds the logic.
The presentation tier is what the user sees and interacts with.
Keeping them distinct is the point.
For object databases, two ideas model complex objects: inheritance and object identity.
Inheritance lets one kind of object build on another.
Object identity gives each object its own identity.
Object-relational databases extend relational systems with richer types, so you keep the relational foundation but gain more expressive data types.
Now the examples of database models and their products, in the order the source gives them.
IBM IMS is hierarchical.
IDMS is network.
PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle are relational.
Redis is key-value.
MongoDB is document.
Cassandra is wide-column.
Neo4j is graph.
And Spanner and CockroachDB are distributed SQL.
Finally, the worked design problem.
Suppose a Student has many courses, and a Course has many students.
That is a many-to-many relationship.
The solution is a bridge table, Enrolment, with the columns StudentID, CourseID and Grade.
It holds the two foreign keys, one pointing to Student and one pointing to Course, and together those two form a composite key.
Composite means the key is made from more than one column combined.
Why is Grade in this bridge table?
Because a grade is an attribute of the association, not of the student or course alone.
A grade only makes sense for a particular student in a particular course.
It belongs to the pairing.
There is also a benefit when data changes.
If a course name is updated, one Course row changes, rather than every enrolment row.
The name is stored once and referenced by key.
And this illustrates why normalisation and referential integrity complement one another.
Normalisation puts each fact in one place.
Referential integrity makes sure the references that connect those places stay valid.
